title: Musk Pitches 200-Mph Hyperloop Tunnel Between Austin and San Antonio
excerpt: The Boring Company founder says the 80-mile Texas tunnel would cut a drive that can take 2.5 hours to under 30 minutes — but revealed no route, cost, or timeline.
body:
• Elon Musk said on X on Sunday that The Boring Company is working on a "simple, precursor Hyperloop" tunnel between Austin and San Antonio, targeting speeds above 200 mph and a sub-30-minute trip.
  • The company disclosed no route, cost, financing structure, timeline, or permits — and past Boring projects in Chicago, Los Angeles, and New York–Washington never materialized.
  • The proposal comes weeks after The Boring Company raised $3 billion in a funding round led by investors from the United Arab Emirates.
  • TxDOT has already flagged Interstate 35, the corridor's main connector, as facing growing congestion with limited room to expand.

Elon Musk said Sunday that his tunneling startup, The Boring Company, is working on a high-speed tunnel between Austin and San Antonio that could carry passengers at more than 200 miles per hour and compress a drive that can now stretch to two and a half hours into a trip of under 30 minutes.

The announcement came in a post on X in which Musk described the project as "a simple, precursor Hyperloop" between the two Texas cities. The Boring Company's own account shared the post and said it "would be excited and honored to build this massive infrastructure project." No route, construction cost, financing structure, expected completion date, or permits were disclosed, and Musk did not say whether the system would use conventional electric vehicles, dedicated passenger pods, or the low-pressure tubes originally envisioned for hyperloop travel.

Context & Background

Musk's comments were, perhaps characteristically, a reply: he re-posted an AI-generated video depicting a science-fiction future of human colonies on other worlds, declaring, "This is the future we shall bring into being," then added the Texas tunnel claim in the replies. The proposal is still at the pitch stage — no government partners or started construction have been identified.

Musk first outlined the hyperloop concept in a 2013 white paper, proposing passenger pods traveling through low-pressure tubes at close to the speed of sound. Several companies tried to commercialize the idea; none now carries paying passengers.

The Boring Company itself has a mixed record on announced megaprojects. Proposed tunnel systems in Chicago, Los Angeles, and between New York City and Washington, D.C., never materialized. Its only working system is the Vegas Loop in Las Vegas, where passengers ride in Tesla cars through tunnels beneath the convention center and the surrounding area. The company began building a tunnel in Nashville this year and plans to start work on a Dubai Loop at the end of 2026. It is also digging tunnels in Bastrop, Texas, to connect properties Musk owns and move staff between Boring, SpaceX, Tesla, and X facilities.

The proposal lands shortly after The Boring Company raised $3 billion in a funding round led by investors from the United Arab Emirates, giving it fresh capital for exactly the kind of large-scale digging this project would demand.

Impact & Analysis

On paper, the pitch has a genuine problem to solve. The two downtowns are roughly 80 miles apart by road, and Musk said traffic congestion can stretch the trip to as long as 2.5 hours. A vehicle averaging 200 mph would cover 80 miles in about 24 minutes, before accounting for acceleration, braking, and station time — so the speed and travel-time claims are at least mathematically consistent. The Texas Department of Transportation has already flagged the corridor as under strain: TxDOT calls Interstate 35 the main connector between the regions, and its Capital-Alamo Connections Study, covering a 12-county region, concluded that population growth will increase congestion while opportunities to widen I-35 are limited.

An 80-mile tunnel at 200 mph would still be a leap beyond anything the company has built. The Vegas Loop is a short, slow urban system; an intercity line would need extensive regulatory approvals, safety testing, and land-access agreements — none of which have been announced. It would also face competition from a passenger rail project already being discussed between the two cities, setting up a three-way contest between highways, rail, and underground travel for the corridor's future.

"We would be excited and honored to build this massive infrastructure project."

— The Boring Company, on X

For investors, the announcement may renew interest in infrastructure tied to Musk's companies, though The Boring Company is privately held. A successful build could open work for construction firms, engineering contractors, and suppliers; another abandoned proposal would join a growing list of Musk infrastructure promises that never left the pitch stage.

Diaspora Angle

The corridor in question runs through the heart of Texas's Indian diaspora boom. Austin's technology scene employs thousands of Indian engineers — including staff at Tesla, SpaceX, X, and Boring itself in nearby Bastrop — and the Austin–San Antonio stretch is one of the fastest-growing regions for Indian-American families in the United States. A tunnel that genuinely tamed I-35 congestion would land as a local quality-of-life story for that community long before it registered as an infrastructure headline.

What's Next

The questions that matter now are bureaucratic, not technological: land rights, environmental review, safety certification, and whether any Texas authority or federal agency is actually in conversation with the company. Watch for filings with TxDOT or the local metropolitan planning organizations that co-authored the corridor's long-term study — and for any sign that the $3 billion in fresh capital is earmarked for a Texas build. Until then, the Austin–San Antonio hyperloop remains what most of Musk's tunnel announcements have been: a compelling reply post awaiting a project plan.
